clue.text: Novelist making a second slip, perhaps

explanation.surface: A writer commits a second blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slip' looks like an error, but it is a close-catching position in cricket; standing at second slip is fielding.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Fielding wrote Tom Jones; in cricket, a player at second slip is out in the field, trying to stop the ball.

clue.text: Supreme Commander to outlaw a — Japanese art

parts.note: Eisenhower, Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, was nicknamed Ike
to outlaw something is to ban it

explanation.surface: A general sets out to prohibit a form of Japanese art.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese art of formal flower arrangement goes by this name.

clue.text: Sovereign gilds these honoured writers

parts.note: a sovereign is a gold pound coin, and L (libra) is the abbreviation for pound
to aureate is to make golden, an old verb from Latin aurum, gold

explanation.surface: A monarch bestows gold upon distinguished authors.
explanation.walkthrough: The sovereign is not a monarch but a pound coin, giving L.
explanation.definitionFit: Poets and writers crowned with laurels for their work, such as the official royal poet, are honoured with this title.

clue.text: Imagine an excerpt from The Bartered Bride (a tense moment)

indicators.note: an excerpt is a piece lifted out of a longer text, so the letters lie within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Picture a dramatic moment in Smetana's comic opera.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'bride a tense', ignoring the bracket.
explanation.definitionFit: To conceive an idea or picture something in the mind is the meaning shared by both words.

clue.text: Berenson's "El Greco of the quattrocento"

parts.note: the art historian Bernard Berenson gave this nickname to a fifteenth-century Sienese painter with elongated, mystical figures

explanation.walkthrough: Quattrocento is the Italian 1400s; Berenson compared this Sienese master's strange expressive style to the later Spanish painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Berenson's famous description singles out this Sienese painter of the fifteenth century.

clue.text: Child holds vestment for Golding's emigrant

indicators.note: the child word grips the vestment word between its letters

parts.note: a tot is a small child
an alb is a long white priestly vestment

explanation.surface: An infant clutches a priest's robe meant for a character in a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund Talbot is the young passenger sailing to Australia in William Golding's Rites of Passage.

clue.text: Thomas treatment of Greene theme lacking power?

definitions.text: Thomas treatment of Greene theme lacking power?

parts.words: Thomas treatment of Greene theme lacking power?
parts.note: Graham Greene's novel title The Power and the ... is trimmed of its 'power' half, giving a book title linked to a Thomas

explanation.walkthrough: Greene's novel is The Power and the Glory; take away the power and this is what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene's whisky-priest novel is The Power and the Glory, so the title without its first noun is what is left.

clue.text: Life of man, according to Hobbes — also poor and nasty

definitions.text: Life of man, according to Hobbes — also poor and nasty

parts.words: Life of man, according to Hobbes — also poor and nasty
parts.note: Hobbes in Leviathan calls life in the state of nature solitary, poor, nasty, ... and short; the clue asks for the missing adjective

explanation.walkthrough: The Leviathan quotation runs 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'; the clue names two neighbours of the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Leviathan, Hobbes lists this savage, beastlike quality among the features of human life without government.

clue.text: Kafka's rook?

parts.note: in chess a rook is also called by the name of a fortress, and Kafka wrote a novel with that fortress as its title

explanation.walkthrough: A rook in chess has another name, the same as the title of Kafka's unfinished novel about the land surveyor K.
explanation.definitionFit: Kafka's novel Das Schloss shares its English title with the chess piece also known as a rook.

clue.text: Swamp explored by Sienkiewicz

explanation.surface: A marsh investigated by a Polish novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swamp' looks like a noun, a marsh; it is the verb, to flood.
explanation.definitionFit: To swamp is to flood or overwhelm; Sienkiewicz's novel Potop, set in the Swedish invasion of Poland, is translated as The Flood or this word.

clue.text: Start of opera is finished and somehow not true

parts.note: something over is finished or ended

indicators.note: the word true is made not true by being put somehow, in a jumbled order

explanation.surface: The opening of an opera is complete and somehow false.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestral prelude played before the curtain rises begins an opera.

clue.text: Training area added in for composer

indicators.note: the composer's name is what the answer becomes once the word in is added, so the word in is taken away from him

parts.note: Palestrina was the Italian Renaissance composer of sacred music

explanation.surface: A practice ground is extended to include a musician.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards from 'for composer': answer with IN added gives the composer, so remove IN from PALESTRINA.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greece a wrestling school or gymnasium was a place for athletic practice.

clue.text: Affectionately, Dolores Haze

parts.note: Humbert Humbert's pet name for the girl Dolores Haze in Nabokov's novel, a Spanish diminutive of Dolores

explanation.definitionFit: Nabokov's narrator calls Dolores Haze by this fond diminutive, which also titles the novel.

clue.text: First daring bet for poet

indicators.note: first signals that only the opening letter of daring is used

parts.note: an ante is a stake put in before cards are dealt

explanation.surface: A bold initial wager is made for a writer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Florentine author of the Divine Comedy is the archetypal Italian poet.

clue.text: Substance abuser who considered murder as a fine art

definitions.text: Substance abuser who considered murder as a fine art

parts.words: Substance abuser who considered murder as a fine art
parts.note: the Confessions of an English Opium-Eater author also wrote the essay On Murder Considered as One of the Fine Arts

explanation.definitionFit: Thomas, the English essayist addicted to laudanum, wrote both the Opium-Eater confessions and the satirical essay on murder as art.

clue.text: The trance possibly produced by dancer's move

indicators.note: possibly says the letters may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A dancer's hypnotic state yields a step.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballet jump in which the feet cross rapidly in the air is a classic leap.

clue.text: Ruck produced this somewhat tender approach to Miss Fayre

definitions.text: Ruck produced this somewhat tender approach to Miss Fayre

parts.words: Ruck produced this somewhat tender approach to Miss Fayre
parts.note: the romantic novelist Berta Ruck wrote a book about the wooing of a Miss Fayre, a tender approach to a lady

explanation.definitionFit: Wooing a lady is a tender approach, and Berta Ruck's romance about Miss Fayre has this word in its title.

clue.text: A politician takes hours in Rome to find vessels

parts.note: MP is a Member of Parliament
horae is the Latin, so Roman, word for hours

explanation.surface: A Member of Parliament spends hours in the Eternal City seeking pots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Rome' asks for the Latin word.
explanation.definitionFit: Two-handled jars used by Greeks and Romans for wine and oil are such containers.

clue.text: Nobel prize poet in surfing move

explanation.surface: A laureate poet is caught up in a wave-riding manoeuvre.
explanation.definitionFit: Salvatore of that surname won the 1959 Nobel prize for literature; surfers also name a hunched crouch on the board after Hugo's bell-ringer.

clue.text: First man with bread was Irish historian

parts.note: Adam is the first man in Genesis
nan, or naan, is a flat Indian bread

explanation.surface: The original human with a loaf turned out to be an Irish chronicler.
explanation.definitionFit: The seventh-century abbot of Iona wrote the life of St Columba, an early Irish chronicle.

clue.text: Composer (not 1) may have a drink before training

parts.note: to sup is to sip or drink
PE is physical education, school training

explanation.surface: A musician may take a drink before exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 'not 1' is printed in the clue; it marks the composer as Franz von Suppé, not the 1-across novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz von Suppé wrote the Light Cavalry and Poet and Peasant overtures.

clue.text: Communications system misrepresenting petrels

indicators.note: misrepresenting shows the word petrels presented in false order

explanation.surface: A network of messages wrongly depicts some seabirds.
explanation.definitionFit: The Post Office's viewdata service sent text pages to television sets over telephone lines.

clue.text: Composer is titled all right

parts.note: Bart is short for baronet, a titled man
OK means all right

explanation.surface: A musician has a title and is fine.
explanation.definitionFit: Béla was the Hungarian who wrote the Concerto for Orchestra.

clue.text: Prophet is first class on the year of Hegira Story in which Wells uncharacteristically lent part

parts.note: A1 means first class, with the 1 as a letter I
AH, anno Hegirae, dates years from Muhammad's flight to Medina

explanation.surface: A holy man is top-rate on Muslim dating.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Testament book of this seer foretells the Messiah.

clue.text: Story in which Wells uncharacteristically lent part

indicators.note: uncharacteristically means not in the usual character or form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: In one tale H. G. Wells took an acting role out of character.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Wells tale the schoolmaster comes back mirror-reversed, so a rearrangement fits.
explanation.definitionFit: The Plattner Story is H. G. Wells's tale of a teacher returned from another dimension left-right inverted.

clue.text: Orchestral piece adds nothing to musical performance

parts.note: a concert is a musical performance
O, the zero shape, is nothing

explanation.surface: A symphonic work gives nothing extra to a recital.
explanation.definitionFit: A work for soloist and orchestra is a staple orchestral composition.

clue.text: Gauguin said that life in that new world was a return to health

definitions.text: Gauguin said that life in that new world was a return to health

parts.words: Gauguin said that life in that new world was a return to health
parts.note: the painter left France for a South Pacific island and wrote that life there restored him

explanation.definitionFit: Gauguin's Polynesian island refuge, where he painted his late works, is meant.

clue.text: Twain's visited Camelot

parts.note: Mark Twain's hero from Connecticut is carried back to King Arthur's court

explanation.definitionFit: Twain's A Connecticut ... in King Arthur's Court sends an American to Camelot.

clue.text: He had the gall to appear in operetta

definitions.text: He had the gall to appear in operetta

parts.words: He had the gall to appear in operetta
parts.note: Robin, hero of Gilbert and Sullivan's Ruddigore, has a surname that names a growth on oak trees, a gall

explanation.walkthrough: 'gall' is not cheek but a plant growth; Robin in Ruddigore bears its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A gall on oak trees and the Ruddigore hero share the name.
